newsitem.title: MEXICO: Central, western Mexico rocked by strong earthquake.
newsitem.headline: Central, western Mexico rocked by strong earthquake.

text.p: A strong earthquake shook western and central Mexico on Saturday afternoon, swaying tall buildings, knocking out power and sparking a few small fires, but apparently causing no major damage in the capital.
Mexico's National Earthquarke Centre reported the quake hit 7.3 on the Richter scale, registering a small aftershock of unknown mangitude about 20 minutes later.

The U.S. Geological Survey in Golden, Colorado, said it made a preliminary estimate of 6.8 for the quake's strength, but geologist Bruce Presgrave told Reuters he thought that would be revised upward in coming weeks.
There was more panic than damage as many Mexicans recalled a pair of huge quakes in September 1985 that destroyed much of central Mexico City, killing thousands of people.

Saturday's tremor was also felt in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara, near where a 488-foot-high (148-meter-high) bridge, one of the largest in the country, was damaged, cutting off the road from Guadalajara to Manzanillo.
"The bridge is seriously damaged, but we have no reports of injuries," Red Cross official Hector Estrada told Reuters.
In Mexico City, traffic lights temporarily malfunctioned, causing abnormal congestion beyond Mexico City's notorious traffic jams, and centuries-old buildings in the historic centre were evacuated.
Mexicans in the centre of town ran out into the streets in panic. A chorus of car alarms were set off by the shaking.

"I felt a lot of fear because I remember September of 1985 when some of my friends and family died," Juan Carillo of Guadalajara told Reuters. "The temblor was still going when I called my family in Mexico City, but luckily everyone was OK."
A few minor fires were caused by severed electrical wires, officials said. Telephone service in the capital was briefly interrupted and some neighbourhoods lost power for hours.
"I was watching television and everything began to shake," said Luis Garcia, an office cleaner in Mexico City. "Suddenly, it rocked violently. It felt terrible."

The tremor's epicentre was under the Pacific Ocean 30 miles (50 km) west-northwest of Playa Azul, in Michoacan state, a survey spokesman said. The fairly sparsely populated area is about 250 miles (410 km) southwest of Mexico City.
"It's a big quake and it lasted a long time," Mexican earthquake centre spokesman Carlos Fuentes told Radio Red.
Some Mexicans said it lasted up to 45 seconds.

The quake hit Mexico City at around 2:30 p.m. local time (2030 GMT) and was felt all over the city, as well as in at least seven states of central and western Mexico including Puebla state, which is east of Mexico City.
The aftershock hit at 2:48 p.m. (2048 GMT), Fuentes said.

After the 1985 quake, a citywide alarm was installed, designed to warn people moments before a big tremor is to hit. But alarms failed to sound, which officials said was because the epicentre was outside the reach of sensors.
Witnesses also said the quake was felt strongly in Michoacan state and in tourist resorts along the Pacific coast in neighbouring Guerrero.
Louis Lichtenstein, a U.S. tourist from Minnesota, told Reuters by telephone from the resort of Ixtapa that the tremor was the strongest he had ever felt.

"The earth shook in a rotational manner with some hard shocks," he said. "We were very glad to be sitting in an open-air restaurant and not in the hotel." Hotel staff said tourists were panicked but had not been hurt.
Miguel Borrego, a Michocan state official, told Reuters 80 percent of the residents in the state's port of Lazaro Cardenas were without water or electricity.
Federal highway officials said two roads in Michoacan were closed by falling rock shaken loose by the quake.
Much of Mexico lies along a geological fault line and feels small earthquakes regularly.
The last strong quake to hit Mexico was on July 15 last year, when a tremor measuring 6.5 on the Richter scale struck southern Mexico, causing panic but no injuries.
